plan: Literary narrative (CLD-P-ACT-R-000011) on a mapmaker's apprenticeship; inference traps where a deliberate omission is fine and the fault is an unexamined choice; R010-04 resubmitted relabelled easy.

passages.title: What Was Left Out
passages.text:
The first thing Master Brandt taught me was that a map is mostly a list of things left out. I had come to his workshop at fourteen expecting to learn how to draw rivers, and for my first month he would not let me draw anything at all. Instead he sent me out with a surveyor's chain and a notebook, and each evening he asked me what I had decided not to record.

I did not understand the question. I had recorded everything I could: the width of the road, the position of each farmhouse, the bend in the stream below the mill. When I said so, he took my notebook, turned a few pages, and asked how many sheep had been in the field behind the church. I told him I had not counted. "Then you decided," he said, "that the sheep did not matter. You were right. But you did not know you were deciding."

It took me a long time to see what he meant. A map of the parish that showed every sheep would be useless, but so would one that showed only the church. Every line was a choice about what a reader would need, and a mapmaker who made those choices without noticing them would make them badly, leaving off a ford because it was small, or drawing a ruined wall because it was large, without asking which one a traveler would care about.

Brandt himself was not an easy man to work for. He corrected my lettering until I hated the alphabet, and he once made me redraw a coastline four times because, he said, I had drawn the sea instead of the shore. But he never corrected a choice without first asking me why I had made it, and he listened to the answer as if it might change his mind. Occasionally it did.

I have made maps for thirty years now. I still hear his question at the end of each day's work, and I still find, more often than I would like to admit, that I have decided something without knowing it.

passages.title: The Option Nobody Wants
passages.text:
Imagine choosing between two subscriptions to a news site: an online-only plan for $59 a year and a print-and-online plan for $125. Many people pick the cheaper plan. Now add a third option, print only, also for $125, and something strange happens. Almost no one chooses print only, yet far more people now choose print-and-online. An option that almost nobody wants has changed what people pick.

Researchers call this the decoy effect. The decoy is designed to be clearly worse than one option (print-and-online gives everything print-only gives, plus more, at the same price) but not clearly worse than the other. Faced with a comparison that is easy to make, people seem to lean toward the option that wins it, even though the decoy tells them nothing new about whether that option is worth its price.

The effect is troubling for a simple model of choice in which people assign each option a value and pick the highest. Under that model, adding an option nobody chooses should not change which of the remaining options is preferred. That it does suggests that people often evaluate options by comparing them with one another rather than judging each on its own merits.

Not every study has found the effect, however. When options are described by many attributes, or when people already hold strong preferences, decoys often have little influence. Some researchers have argued that the effect appears most reliably in laboratory tasks with simple, numerical descriptions, and that its importance in everyday decisions may have been overstated.

Even so, businesses appear to have taken the lesson to heart. Menus, software plans, and appliance lineups often include an option whose main purpose seems to be making a neighbor look attractive. Whether those decoys work as well in the store as they do in the laboratory is a question the research has not yet settled.

choices.A: the narrator's struggle to master the technical skills of lettering and drawing.
choices.B: a lasting conflict between the narrator and a demanding teacher that was never resolved.
choices.C: how the narrator came to grasp a teacher's lesson that mapping means choosing what to omit.
choices.D: the history of how the narrator's parish was surveyed and mapped over many years.

candidates.evidence: a map is mostly a list of things left out
candidates.explanation: The passage opens with Brandt's lesson, shows the narrator's confusion and gradual understanding, and ends with the lesson still shaping the narrator's work.

A.rationale: Lettering appears briefly; the passage centers on the lesson about choices.

B.rationale: The narrator respects Brandt and still follows his lesson.

D.rationale: The parish is only the setting for the lesson.

hints: What lesson frames the first and last paragraphs?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the arc in one sentence first.

candidates.remember: A main idea must cover the passage's whole arc.

candidates.stem: When Brandt says, "You were right. But you did not know you were deciding" (paragraph 2), he most likely means that the narrator:

choices.A: made a sound omission without realizing that it was a choice.
choices.B: should have counted the sheep after all, since every detail matters.
choices.C: had recorded so many details that the notebook was nearly useless.
choices.D: had been careless in measuring the width of the road and the stream.

candidates.explanation: Brandt approves the omission ("You were right") but points out that it was an unconscious choice ("you did not know you were deciding").

B.rationale: "You were right" confirms that leaving out the sheep was correct.

C.rationale: Brandt's point is not that there were too many details, but that the narrator chose without noticing.

D.rationale: Brandt raises no complaint about the measurements.

strategy.explanation: Read both halves of the quotation.

candidates.remember: A quotation with "but" often approves one thing and criticizes another.

candidates.stem: The examples of the ford and the ruined wall in paragraph 3 mainly serve to:

choices.A: show that small features on a map are always less important than large ones.
choices.B: describe features that Brandt specifically asked the narrator to record on surveys.
choices.C: contrast the maps the narrator made with the maps Brandt himself had made.
choices.D: show how unexamined choices could lead a mapmaker to include or omit the wrong features.

candidates.evidence: without asking which one a traveler would care about
candidates.explanation: The small but useful ford might be dropped and the large but useless wall kept, the errors of a mapmaker who chooses without noticing.

A.rationale: The examples suggest the opposite: a small ford may matter more than a large wall.

B.rationale: Brandt never asks for these features.

hints: Why might a careless mapmaker drop the ford and keep the wall?

strategy.explanation: Read the clause that follows the examples.

candidates.remember: Examples usually illustrate the claim right before them.

candidates.stem: When Brandt complains that the narrator "had drawn the sea instead of the shore" (paragraph 4), he most likely means that the narrator:

choices.A: used an ink for the water that was much too dark for the rest of the map.
choices.B: gave attention to the wrong feature instead of the edge the map needed to show.
choices.C: placed the coastline several miles from where it actually lay.
choices.D: worked so slowly on the coastline that the map was finished late.

candidates.evidence: Every line was a choice about what a reader would need
candidates.explanation: In keeping with the passage's lesson about choosing what matters, the complaint is that the narrator attended to the sea rather than the shoreline, the feature a map must render.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests the line was misplaced; the complaint is about what was emphasized.

hints: How does this complaint connect to Brandt's main lesson?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate readings the passage does not support.

candidates.remember: Interpret figurative lines through the passage's central idea.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, during the narrator's first month in the workshop Brandt:

choices.A: had the narrator survey and take notes rather than draw.
choices.B: taught the narrator to draw rivers, roads, and farmhouses.
choices.C: made the narrator redraw a coastline four separate times.
choices.D: asked the narrator to count the livestock in every field.

candidates.evidence: for my first month he would not let me draw anything at all
candidates.explanation: In the first month Brandt sent the narrator out with a chain and notebook and would not allow drawing.

B.rationale: He "would not let me draw anything at all" that month.

C.rationale: The coastline episode is described later, not in the first month.

D.rationale: He asked about the sheep to make a point, not as an assignment.

strategy.explanation: Match the time frame in the question.

candidates.remember: Check that a detail belongs to the time the question names.

candidates.stem: The narrator's description of Brandt in paragraph 4 suggests that Brandt was:

choices.A: harsh in every respect and unwilling to hear any explanation.
choices.B: patient about lettering but rigid about the narrator's choices.
choices.C: exacting about technique yet genuinely open to the narrator's reasons.
choices.D: more concerned with coastlines than with any other feature.

candidates.evidence: he listened to the answer as if it might change his mind
candidates.explanation: Brandt corrected lettering relentlessly but asked and listened before correcting choices: exacting yet open.

A.rationale: He listened to the narrator's reasons "as if it might change his mind."

B.rationale: This reverses the description: strict about lettering, open about choices.

D.rationale: The coastline is one example of his strictness.

strategy.explanation: Look for both sides of the description.

candidates.subskill: Relationship of the conclusion to the passage
candidates.stem: Which choice best describes how the final paragraph relates to the rest of the passage?

choices.A: It shows that Brandt's question still shapes the narrator's work and remains hard to answer.
choices.B: It reveals that the narrator eventually stopped making maps and chose another trade.
choices.C: It explains why the narrator came to reject Brandt's way of teaching apprentices.
choices.D: It introduces a new lesson that contradicts what Brandt had taught the narrator.

candidates.evidence: I still hear his question at the end of each day's work
candidates.explanation: Thirty years later the narrator still asks Brandt's question and still sometimes decides without knowing, which shows the lesson's lasting force and difficulty.

B.rationale: The narrator has made maps for thirty years.

C.rationale: The narrator still hears and values his question.

hints: What does the narrator still do at the end of each day?

strategy.explanation: Connect the last paragraph to the first.

candidates.remember: Endings often show how a lesson lasted.

candidates.stem: Based on the passage, Brandt would most likely judge a map to be poor if it:

choices.A: included details chosen without thought for what a reader would need.
choices.B: left out features that the mapmaker had deliberately judged unimportant.
choices.C: showed fewer features than the land it represented actually contained.
choices.D: had lettering that was neat but simple and without decoration.

candidates.evidence: a mapmaker who made those choices without noticing them would make them badly
candidates.explanation: For Brandt, omission is normal; the fault is choosing without considering the reader. A map built on unexamined choices fails his standard.

B.rationale: Brandt approves deliberate omissions, like leaving out the sheep.

C.rationale: Every map leaves things out; that is Brandt's first lesson.

D.rationale: Brandt cares about lettering being correct, not decorated.

hints: Is leaving things out a problem for Brandt?
What does he say makes choices bad?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that Brandt would accept.

candidates.remember: Apply the character's stated standard, not a common-sense one.

candidates.stem: The phrase "Occasionally it did" (paragraph 4) suggests that:

choices.A: the narrator's lettering sometimes improved after Brandt corrected it.
choices.B: the narrator sometimes redrew coastlines more than four times.
choices.C: Brandt sometimes changed his view after hearing the narrator's reasons.
choices.D: Brandt seldom bothered to listen to anything the narrator said.

candidates.evidence: he listened to the answer as if it might change his mind
candidates.explanation: "It" refers to the narrator's answer changing Brandt's mind; "occasionally" means this sometimes happened.

A.rationale: "It" refers to the narrator's answer, not the lettering.

D.rationale: He listened "as if it might change his mind."

candidates.remember: Pin down what a pronoun refers to.

candidates.stem: According to the simple model of choice described in paragraph 3, adding the print-only plan should have:

choices.A: increased the share of people choosing the print-and-online plan.
choices.B: left people's preferences between the other two plans unchanged.
choices.C: caused many people to switch to the new print-only plan instead.
choices.D: made people judge each plan by comparing it with the other plans.

candidates.evidence: adding an option nobody chooses should not change which of the remaining options is preferred
candidates.explanation: The simple model scores each option independently, so an unchosen option should not shift preferences among the others.

A.rationale: That is what actually happened, which is why the effect troubles the model.

C.rationale: The model predicts no change among the others; it says nothing about print-only being popular.

D.rationale: Comparing options is what the passage contrasts with the simple model.

hints: What does the simple model say about adding an unchosen option?

strategy.explanation: Separate what the model predicts from what actually occurred.

candidates.remember: Keep a model's prediction separate from the observed result.
candidates.revision_note: R010-04 resubmitted unchanged in content and relabelled easy after both blind solvers rated it easy (70-75%).
